definition: Equivocal means deliberately ambiguous or vague, especially in wording chosen to avoid committing to a clear position.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word equivocal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know equivocal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When shareholders demanded a yes or no on the buyout, the chairman gave an equivocal reply that left both sides guessing.
A noncommittal answer simply declines to take a side, while an equivocal one is deliberately worded so it can be read more than one way.
Equivocal language leaves a speaker's real position unclear, but duplicitous speech goes further, actively saying one thing while intending another.

Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation, and it carries no verdict about intent - a mumbled instruction or a badly placed comma can be ambiguous by pure accident. Equivocal adds calculation: the wording was chosen so it cannot be pinned down. Every equivocal answer is ambiguous, but only the deliberate ones are equivocal.

Evasive means deliberately avoiding a direct answer - dodging, changing the subject, pleading ignorance. An evasive speaker escapes the question; an equivocal one answers it, in words engineered to face both directions at once. Evasion leaves you with no answer; equivocation leaves you with two.

Equivocal means deliberately ambiguous or vague, especially in wording chosen to avoid committing to a clear position.
During a live interview, a tech executive was asked whether her company would cut jobs after the merger.

She answered that the company 'always evaluates every option to serve our teams best.' Reporters replayed the clip for days, some hearing a promise of no layoffs, others hearing a warning of cuts to come.
Her equivocal answer let listeners on both sides believe she agreed with them, which was exactly the point.
The executive's statement was deliberately worded so it could be read in opposite ways, letting her avoid committing to a clear position, which is what equivocal means.
formal, often critical register
Equivocal typically describes answers, statements, responses, and results (an equivocal answer, equivocal test results).
It describes the wording itself, not the person, and it usually implies the vagueness is deliberate; something merely unclear by accident is better called ambiguous.

Ancient Greece's most famous fortune-teller, the oracle at Delphi, owed part of her long career to careful grammar.
When King Croesus asked whether he should invade Persia, the priestess answered that if he crossed the river, a great empire would fall.
Croesus marched, lost everything, and learned too late that the equivocal prophecy fit his own empire as neatly as his enemy's.
Historians note the pattern: the shrine's answers were routinely worded so that any outcome could be read back into them as foresight.
A prophecy that cannot be wrong, of course, is also one that commits to nothing — a bargain visitors seemed happy to accept.
